cues.caption: Welcome back, champ!
cues.text: Hey champ, welcome back! Ready for some more maths fun?

cues.caption: Last time: 101 → 4 + 0 + 1 = 5
cues.text: Last time, we counted the computer way, with lamps that are on or off. Remember? One, zero, one, was four plus one. Five!

cues.caption: Chapter 2 · Odd, Even, and Patterns
cues.text: Today is chapter two of Numbers Computers Love. It's called, Odd, Even, and Patterns!

cues.caption: Share, hop, and clap!
cues.text: We'll share some laddoos, hop along a number line, and even clap out a pattern. Let's go!

cues.caption: Riya shares laddoos: two on every plate
cues.text: Meet Riya. It's Diwali, and Nani has made a big box of laddoos. Riya's job is to share them out, two laddoos on every plate.

cues.caption: 8 laddoos → 4 pairs, none left over
cues.text: First, she has eight laddoos. Two, four, six, eight. That's four plates, with nothing left over. Perfect!

cues.caption: 7 laddoos → 3 pairs and 1 left over
cues.text: The next day, there are seven laddoos. Two, four, six, and, oh no! One laddoo is left all alone, with no partner.

cues.caption: Why is one laddoo left over? Think!
cues.text: Hmm. Why do some numbers share perfectly into pairs, while others always leave one behind? Think about it.

cues.caption: Two kinds of numbers. Let's name them!
cues.text: Here's the secret. Every number is one of two kinds. And each kind has a special name.

cues.caption: EVEN: makes pairs, nothing left over
cues.text: A number that splits into pairs, with nothing left over, is called an even number. Every laddoo has a partner. So eight is even.

cues.caption: ODD: one left over
cues.text: A number that leaves one left over, when you make pairs, is called an odd number. One laddoo has no partner. So seven is odd.

cues.caption: Every whole number is odd OR even
cues.text: Every whole number is either odd, or even. Never both, and never neither!

cues.caption: Pairs test: make pairs, see what's left
cues.text: So here's a simple test. Make pairs, and see if anything is left. Let's try it.

cues.caption: 6 → 3 pairs, none left → EVEN
cues.text: Six. Three pairs, and nothing left over. So six is even.

cues.caption: 9 → 4 pairs + 1 left → ODD
cues.text: Nine. Four pairs, and one left over. So nine is odd.

cues.caption: 11 → 5 pairs + 1 left → ODD
cues.text: And what if Riya has eleven laddoos? Five pairs, and one left over. So eleven is odd too.

cues.caption: Big number? Just look at the last digit!
cues.text: But what about a big number, like thirty-eight? Making pairs would take forever! Here's a quick trick. Just look at the last digit.

cues.caption: Ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 → EVEN
cues.text: If the last digit is zero, two, four, six, or eight, the number is even.

cues.caption: Ends in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 → ODD
cues.text: If it's one, three, five, seven, or nine, the number is odd.

cues.caption: 38 ends in 8 → even · 25 ends in 5 → odd
cues.text: So thirty-eight ends in eight. It's even! And twenty-five ends in five. It's odd!

cues.caption: Tens always make pairs, so the last digit decides
cues.text: Why does this trick work? Because tens always split into pairs perfectly. Thirty is fifteen pairs. So only the last digit decides!

cues.caption: 1 to 20: odd in orange, even in green
cues.text: Now let's line up the numbers from one to twenty. Odd numbers in orange, and even numbers in green.

cues.caption: Odd, even, odd, even… they take turns!
cues.text: Look at that! Odd, even, odd, even. They take turns, all the way along. Just like your feet when you walk. Left, right, left, right.

cues.caption: How many odd numbers from 1 to 10?
cues.text: Here's a question. How many odd numbers are there, from one to ten? Count them.

cues.caption: Five! 1, 3, 5, 7, 9
cues.text: Five! One, three, five, seven, and nine. And there are five even numbers too. Two, four, six, eight, and ten.

cues.caption: Tinku the frog skips every other number
cues.text: Now meet Tinku, Riya's pet frog. Tinku loves hopping along the number line. But he always skips every other number.

cues.caption: Start at 2: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 → evens
cues.text: Start at two, and skip one each time. Two, four, six, eight, ten. Tinku lands only on even numbers!

cues.caption: Start at 1: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 → odds
cues.text: Now start at one. One, three, five, seven, nine. This time, he lands only on odd numbers.

cues.caption: Start at 1… will Tinku land on 20?
cues.text: So, if Tinku starts at one and keeps hopping, will he ever land on twenty? What do you think?

cues.caption: No! 20 is even. He lands on 19, then 21
cues.text: No! Starting at one, he only lands on odd numbers. Twenty is even, so he hops right over it. Nineteen, then twenty-one.

cues.caption: The rule: add 2 each time
cues.text: Tinku's hops make a number pattern. Each number is two more than the one before. So the rule is, add two.
Two, four, six, eight. What comes next? Pause, and think.
Ten! Eight plus two equals ten.
Here's another one. Ten, twelve, fourteen. What comes next?
Sixteen! Fourteen plus two equals sixteen. You're a pattern pro!

cues.caption: A pattern repeats by a rule: clap, snap…
cues.text: Patterns aren't only numbers. A pattern is anything that repeats by a rule. Like this. Clap, snap. Clap, snap.

cues.caption: Clap, snap, clap, snap, clap, ___?
cues.text: Clap, snap, clap, snap, clap, and then? What comes next?

cues.caption: Snap! They take turns, like odd and even
cues.text: Snap! Clap and snap take turns, just like odd and even numbers do.

cues.caption: Clap on the even numbers: 2, 4, 6, 8
cues.text: Now let's mix in numbers. Count to eight, and clap only on the even ones. One, two, clap. Three, four, clap. Five, six, clap. Seven, eight, clap!

cues.caption: Code loves rules that repeat!
cues.text: Computers love patterns too. A rule that repeats is how code does a job again and again, without ever getting bored.

cues.caption: 7, 12, 15, 20, 3, 18: which are even?
cues.text: Sorting time! Seven, twelve, fifteen, twenty, three, and eighteen. Which ones go in the even basket? Use the last digit trick.

cues.caption: Even: 12, 20, 18 · Odd: 7, 15, 3
cues.text: Twelve, twenty, and eighteen are even. They end in two, zero, and eight. Seven, fifteen, and three are odd. Brilliant sorting!

cues.caption: Your turn: practice check
cues.text: Okay champ, practice check time, just like the quiz.

cues.caption: Is 14 odd or even? How do you know?
cues.text: Is fourteen odd, or even? And how do you know? Pause the video, and try it on paper.

cues.caption: Even! 7 pairs, none left over, ends in 4
cues.text: Fourteen is even! It makes seven pairs, with nothing left over. And it ends in four. Two ways to know. Super!

cues.caption: Even = pairs, nothing left over
cues.text: Let's remember. Even numbers make pairs, with nothing left over.

cues.caption: Odd = one left over
cues.text: Odd numbers always have one left over.

cues.caption: Last digit 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 → even
cues.text: Check the last digit. Zero, two, four, six, or eight means even.

cues.caption: Patterns repeat by a rule
cues.text: And patterns repeat by a rule, like add two, or clap, snap.

cues.caption: Chapter 2 done!
cues.text: Chapter two, done! You can sort odd and even, and spot patterns. Super work, champ!

cues.text: Now let's see what you remember. Tap Finish, and try the quiz. You've got this!
